why: A 512-token runbook whose only difference is in a final paragraph the encoder never reads. The two blocks embed to byte-identical vectors (measured), so similarity says nothing at all here and the guard's full-text reading is the only thing that can accept or refuse it. This is the positive counterpart of adversarial_negative/truncation-boundary-negation.

canonical_text: Payments API incident runbook, revision 7.
Scope. This runbook covers the checkout service and the two dependencies it
cannot serve a request without: the ledger service and the settlement queue.
It does not cover the merchant dashboard, which keeps its own runbook, and it
does not cover planned maintenance windows, which are announced a week ahead
and handled by the release captain rather than by whoever holds the pager.
Severity. Declare a Sev-1 when the checkout success rate stays below ninety
percent for five consecutive minutes, or when settlement lag passes fifteen
minutes. Declare a Sev-2 when one region degrades while global checkout
success stays healthy, or when a dependency is failing but retries are
absorbing it. Everything else is a Sev-3 and waits for business hours. The
severity is set by whoever is paged and revised by the incident commander;
nobody needs permission to raise it, and lowering it is the commander's call
alone.
First response. Acknowledge the page within five minutes. Open an incident
channel and post three things into it: the dashboard link, the alert that
fired, and the timestamp it fired at. Do not start remediation before the
channel exists. The timeline that channel produces is what the post-incident
review reads, and a fix applied before anyone was writing things down leaves
no record of what the system looked like when it broke.
Triage. Check four signals, in this order, because each one rules out the
next. First the deploy timeline: a change that shipped in the last thirty
minutes is both the likeliest cause and the fastest thing to undo. Second the
ledger service error rate, because that dependency fails more often than
everything else combined. Third the settlement queue depth, which grows
quietly for a long time and only becomes visible once consumers have already
fallen behind. Fourth the connection pool saturation on the primary database,
which presents as a checkout problem and almost never is one.
Rollback. A rollback of the checkout service is always safe, because every
release is backward compatible with the previous schema and that property is
enforced in continuous integration rather than remembered by a person. The
same is not true of the ledger service, whose migrations run one way only.
Roll the ledger service back with the database owner on the call, never on
your own authority, and never while a settlement batch is mid-flight.
Communication. Update the incident channel every fifteen minutes even when
nothing at all has changed, because silence reads as an unattended incident
to everyone who is not in the room with you. The incident commander owns the
update and may delegate it explicitly, in writing, in the channel. Nobody
posts to the customer-facing status page except the commander.
Handover. An incident that outlives a shift is handed over in the channel and
not in a private message. The incoming commander confirms in writing that
they hold the timeline, the current hypothesis, and the list of every change
already applied. The outgoing commander stays reachable for thirty minutes
after the handover in case the written record turns out to be missing
something the room knew and never said out loud.
Escalation. Page the payments director when an incident passes 120 minutes.
